items.stimulus:
Every weeknight in thousands of homes, a familiar scene unfolds. A seven-year-old sits at the kitchen table with a worksheet, a tired parent hovers nearby, and what should be a quiet evening turns into a negotiation. We are told that this ritual builds discipline and raises achievement. For children in primary school, I believe it does neither, and it should be abolished.

Start with achievement. Studies of older students find a modest link between homework and test results, but among children under eleven the link largely disappears. A worksheet of thirty sums does little that the same thirty sums done in class, with a teacher on hand to correct mistakes, could not do better. At home, an error practised thirty times is simply an error learned thirty times.

Then consider what homework displaces. The hours after school are when young children play outside, read for pleasure, help to cook a meal or simply get bored enough to invent something. These activities are not idle. They build the language, curiosity and self-control on which later learning depends. An hour of homework is an hour taken from them.

Homework also widens the gap it claims to close. A child whose parent is home in the evening, confident with fractions and fluent in the language of instruction, gets a private tutor. A child whose parent works night shifts gets an unfinished sheet and a reprimand the next morning. The task is the same; the help is not.

Defenders say that homework teaches responsibility. But responsibility is better learned by caring for a pet, packing one's own school bag or keeping a promise to a friend than by completing exercises that a seven-year-old did not choose and cannot see the point of. Indeed, my neighbour's two children never had homework at their school, and both grew into conscientious adults, which shows that homework is unnecessary for developing good habits.

Schools should keep the school day for schoolwork and give evenings back to families. If teachers want children to read at home, they can send home good books, not worksheets.
items.question: Which one of the following best expresses the main point of the essay?

options.text: Homework is useful for older students and should simply be shortened, not removed, for primary-school children.
Homework for primary-school children should be abolished because its benefits are weak and its costs are real.
Parents should take a more active part in the evenings, helping young children to understand and complete their homework.
Outdoor play matters more than reading for the development of children under eleven.

items.question: During which one-hour period did the greatest number of visitors enter the shop?

items.question: If Gideon is selected, which one of the following must be true?

Kemal is selected.

items.stimulus: A sailing club has 9 members: 5 women and 4 men. Among the women is Rosa; among the men is Tomas. The club needs to choose people from its members for various roles. Unless a question says otherwise, a committee is a group of people in which the order of choosing does not matter, and any member may be chosen.
items.question: A committee of 3 is to be chosen from the 9 members. How many different committees include at least one woman and at least one man?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 전체 3인 위원회 수는 9C3 = 84이다. 2) 여성만 있는 경우 5C3 = 10, 남성만 있는 경우 4C3 = 4이다. 3) 84 - 10 - 4 = 70이다. 검산: 여2남1 = 10×4 = 40, 여1남2 = 5×6 = 30, 합 70. 오답: A 조건을 무시한 전체 수다. C 여성만 있는 경우(10)만 뺐다. D 남성만 있는 경우(4)만 뺐다. E 여2남1 경우만 셌다. 유형 팁: '적어도 하나' 조건은 전체에서 조건을 만족하지 않는 경우를 빼는 여사건이 빠르다. → 정답 B

items.explanation_ko: 1) 제한 없는 3인 위원회는 9C3 = 84개다. 2) Rosa와 Tomas가 함께 들어가는 위원회는 나머지 1명을 7명 중에서 고르는 7가지다. 3) 84 - 7 = 77이다. 오답: A 7C3으로 두 사람을 모두 빼 버린 수다. B 8C3으로 한 사람을 아예 제외한 수다. C 84에서 7C2 = 21을 빼는 실수다. 유형 팁: '함께 있으면 안 된다'는 함께 있는 경우만 세어 전체에서 뺀다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus:
The visible spectrum is continuous: light shades from red to violet with no natural borders between one colour and the next. Yet every language cuts this continuum into named pieces, and languages do not all cut it in the same places. Some have only a handful of basic colour words; others have a dozen or more. Many languages use a single basic term covering both what English speakers call green and what they call blue, while Russian treats light blue and dark blue as two basic colours rather than as shades of one.

Such differences were once taken as proof that language shapes perception: if you have no word for a boundary, perhaps you cannot see it. Later experiments complicated the picture. Speakers of languages with one green-blue term can still tell a green chip from a blue one when the two are placed side by side. What differs is subtler. When asked to pick the odd one out among three chips, people respond slightly faster if the odd chip falls on the other side of a boundary that their own language names. This advantage shrinks when they are asked, at the same time, to repeat a string of numbers aloud, a task that occupies verbal memory.

The pattern of naming is not random either. Across many unrelated languages, a term for red tends to appear before terms for green or yellow, and terms for brown or purple tend to appear only once several others are in place. Such regularities suggest that the colour vocabulary of a language is shaped both by the eye, which all humans share, and by the needs and history of the people who speak it.

items.stimulus:
Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was costly and complicated. Charges depended on the distance travelled and the number of sheets, and they were normally paid not by the sender but by the person receiving the letter. A long-distance letter could cost a large share of a labourer's daily wage. Post Office clerks spent much of their time calculating charges and collecting coins at the door, and recipients sometimes refused letters they did not wish to pay for. Some correspondents exploited this: by agreeing on small marks on the outside of a letter, they could send a message that the recipient read at a glance before handing the unopened letter back.

In 1837 a schoolmaster and reformer, Rowland Hill, published a pamphlet arguing that the system was wasteful. Hill calculated that the cost of actually carrying a letter was tiny compared with the cost of handling and accounting for it. If postage were cheap, the same everywhere in the country and paid in advance, he argued, the work of collection would almost disappear and far more people would write. To show that a letter had been paid for, he proposed a small printed label that the sender would stick on the letter.

Parliament adopted a uniform rate of one penny for letters weighing up to half an ounce, and in May 1840 the first adhesive postage stamp, printed in black with a profile of the young Queen Victoria, went on sale. The number of letters sent roughly doubled within a year. Revenue, however, fell sharply at first and took many years to return to its earlier level, and critics who had predicted a financial loss felt that they had been proved right. Yet within a few decades many other countries had introduced prepaid stamps of their own.

items.stimulus:
Moral relativism, in its simplest form, holds that an action is right or wrong only relative to the standards of a particular culture. On this view there is no neutral vantage point from which one society's practices can be judged better or worse than another's; to call a foreign custom 'wrong' is merely to report that it conflicts with one's own customs.

The view has an attractive motive. History offers many examples of travellers and empires condemning practices they did not understand, often as an excuse for domination. Relativism seems to counsel humility: before judging, remember that your own standards are themselves the product of a particular time and place.

But the simple form faces serious difficulties. First, if rightness just is conformity to a culture's standards, then reformers within a culture are wrong by definition. A person who campaigned against a practice that most of her society accepted would be mistaken simply because she was in the minority, and her later success would mean only that the standards had changed, not that they had improved. Few relativists are willing to say that moral progress is impossible.

Second, the relativist's own call for humility is not relative. When relativists say that we ought to tolerate other cultures, they seem to state a principle that applies everywhere, including in cultures whose standards reject tolerance. The theory thus appears to rely on at least one value that it cannot explain.

None of this shows that every moral disagreement has a clear answer, or that outsiders always understand a practice well enough to judge it. But disagreement about a question does not show that it has no answer: people once disagreed about the shape of the earth. What these difficulties suggest is that humility is best understood as a moral virtue in its own right, a reason to judge carefully, rather than as a reason to stop judging altogether.

A census looks like the most neutral of government activities: officials count people and publish the totals. In practice, almost every step of counting involves choices, and those choices can carry political weight.

The first choice is who counts as a resident of a place. Should students be counted where they study or where their families live? items.stimulus:
When a human driver causes a crash, we usually know whom to hold responsible. When a car drives itself, the answer is less obvious. Several parties have a claim to the role: the manufacturer that designed the driving software, the owner who chose to use it, and the person in the driver's seat who might have intervened.

One view holds that responsibility should rest mainly with manufacturers. They alone understand how the software makes decisions, they profit from selling it, and they are best placed to make it safer. If they bear the cost of crashes, the argument runs, they will have a strong incentive to prevent them. Owners, by contrast, cannot inspect millions of lines of code and should not be blamed for trusting a product that was approved for sale.

A second view stresses the person in the car. Most current systems require a human to stay alert and take control when warned. On this view, a person who reads a book while the car steers has accepted a risk, just as a passenger who distracts a driver shares some of the blame.

Both views face a difficulty. Systems that work well almost all of the time encourage people to stop paying attention, so the rare moment when a human must intervene is the moment the human is least ready. Blaming the occupant for failing at a task that the system has made almost impossible seems unfair. Yet placing all responsibility on manufacturers may also go too far: an owner who ignores repeated warnings or disables safety features has made a choice that no designer controlled.

A defensible approach, then, may divide responsibility according to who could reasonably have prevented the harm. Where a crash results from a design fault that the occupant could not have detected or corrected, the manufacturer should answer for it. Where the occupant ignored clear warnings that a reasonable person would have heeded, at least part of the responsibility shifts to the occupant.

items.stimulus:
A town council is deciding whether images made with AI image generators should be allowed in its annual public art competition. Four people give their views.

Speaker 1 (competition judge): "This competition exists to reward artistic vision, not manual skill. Photographers were once told their work was not art because a machine made the image. If an entrant uses an image generator to realise an idea no one else had, the idea is what we should judge. We should allow AI images, provided entrants declare how they were made."

Speaker 2 (painter): "Image generators are trained on millions of pictures made by artists who were never asked and never paid. Entering a generator's output in a competition rewards the entrant for work taken from others. Until those artists consent, AI images have no place in a public prize funded by ratepayers."

Speaker 3 (art teacher): "My students spend years learning to draw. If an image produced from a sentence typed in thirty seconds can win the same prize, young people will conclude that the effort is pointless. A competition sends a message about what a community values. Create a separate category for AI images, so that both can be celebrated without one discouraging the other."

Speaker 4 (council arts officer): "A ban sounds simple but cannot be enforced. Many artists already use digital tools with some automated features, and judges cannot reliably tell the difference. Any rule we adopt must be one we can actually check; otherwise honest entrants follow it while others quietly ignore it."
items.question: Speaker 3's proposal differs from Speaker 1's mainly because Speaker 3

options.text: thinks that AI images should be banned from the competition entirely, whether or not they are declared.
believes that images made by AI generators cannot be considered art.
is concerned with how AI entries affect people learning traditional skills, not with how ideas should be judged.
worries that any rule about AI images would be impossible to enforce because judges cannot tell them apart.

items.stimulus:
A ship sends signals by hanging flags one above another on a mast. There are five different flags: red, yellow, blue, green and white. A signal is a column of either 2 or 3 different flags, read from top to bottom, so the same flags in a different order form a different signal. No flag can appear twice in one signal. Two further rules apply:
1. The white flag is never at the top.
2. The red flag and the green flag are never directly next to each other.
items.question: How many different 2-flag signals are possible?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 규칙이 없으면 서로 다른 2개를 순서대로 고르는 5 × 4 = 20가지다. 2) 흰색이 위에 오는 4가지를 빼면 16가지다. 3) 빨강-초록, 초록-빨강의 2가지는 인접 금지에 걸리고 흰색 위 경우와 겹치지 않으므로 빼면 14가지다. 오답: B 규칙 2를 적용하지 않았다. C 규칙을 모두 무시했다. D 빨강·초록 인접을 4가지로 두 번 뺐다. 유형 팁: 여러 제한 조건을 뺄 때는 조건끼리 겹치는 경우가 있는지 확인한다. → 정답 A
